# Clean and standardise text {#sec-uc-clean}



Most matching problems are really cleaning problems. Two records for the
same business rarely differ by a typo; they differ by `&` against `&`,
`St.` against `Street`, `Müller` against `Mueller`, or a postcode that lost
its leading zero on the way through a spreadsheet. This chapter collects the
functions that remove that noise, each of them one vectorised, multi-core
call.

| Task | Function | Instead of |
|---|---|---|
| Decode `&`, `é`, `–` | `html_unescape()` | `xml2` one string at a time, or nothing |
| Decode `%20`, `+` in URLs and query strings | `url_decode()` | `utils::URLdecode()` (R code, per string) |
| Trim and collapse all Unicode whitespace | `fsquish()` | `stringr::str_squish()` |
| Accents and typographic symbols to ASCII | `ascii_fold()` | `stringi::stri_trans_general(x, "Latin-ASCII")` |
| Replace whole words from a dictionary | `freplace_tokens()` | `strsplit()` + `match()` + `paste()` |
| Restore leading zeros, fixed widths | `fpad()` | `stringr::str_pad()`, `formatC()` |
| Group spelling variants | `fingerprint()`, `ngram_fingerprint()` | OpenRefine's key collision clustering |

## Web residue: entities, escapes and odd spaces

Text that has passed through a web page, a CMS export or a JSON API often
arrives with HTML character references still in it, and with non-breaking
or ideographic spaces where you expect ordinary ones.
`html_unescape()` decodes every named and numeric reference of the HTML
standard -- exactly as Python's `html.unescape()` does -- and `fsquish()`
trims and collapses every kind of Unicode whitespace:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
scraped <- c("  Caf\u00e9\u00a0Nero ", "Fish & Chips\tCo.",
             "O\u2019Brien – Plumbing", "M\u00fcller\u3000GmbH",
             "Smith & Sons", "PLAIN NAME")
fsquish(html_unescape(scraped))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Café Nero"          "Fish & Chips Co."   "O’Brien – Plumbing" "Müller GmbH"        "Smith & Sons"       "PLAIN NAME"        
```


:::
:::


` ` decodes to a non-breaking space, which is why `fsquish()` runs
second. Strings without an `&` are returned untouched (not even copied), so
running `html_unescape()` over a column that is mostly clean costs almost
nothing.

Web logs and exported URLs carry percent-encoding instead. Pull out the part
you need with `fextract()` and decode it; `plus = TRUE` treats `+` as a
space, as HTML forms encode it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
logs <- c("/search?q=fish+%26+chips&page=2", "/search?q=caf%C3%A9+latte",
          "/search?page=1&q=100%25+beef", "/about")
q <- fextract("[?&]q=([^&]*)", logs, group = 1)
data.frame(q, decoded = url_decode(q, plus = TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                q      decoded
1  fish+%26+chips fish & chips
2 caf%C3%A9+latte   café latte
3     100%25+beef    100% beef
4            <NA>         <NA>
```


:::
:::


`url_encode()` goes the other way, with `reserved = TRUE` for a single
query value. Both agree with `utils::URLencode()`/`URLdecode()` -- except
that a broken escape such as `%zz` is kept as it is rather than turned into
garbage -- and are several hundred times faster, because the base functions
loop over characters in R code.

## Accents and typographic symbols

Names keyed on different systems disagree about accents: one has
`François Müller`, another `Francois Muller`. `ascii_fold()` applies the
same Latin-to-ASCII transliteration as ICU (and `stringi`), including
ligatures, Nordic letters and typographic punctuation:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names <- c("Fran\u00e7ois M\u00fcller", "Zo\u00eb \u00c6lfric",
           "Bj\u00f6rk Gu\u00f0mundsd\u00f3ttir", "\u0141\u00f3d\u017a",
           "\u201cQuoted\u201d \u2013 dash", "\u00bd price \u2026")
data.frame(names, folded = ascii_fold(names))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                 names               folded
1      François Müller      Francois Muller
2           Zoë Ælfric          Zoe AElfric
3 Björk Guðmundsdóttir Bjork Gudmundsdottir
4                 Łódź                 Lodz
5      “Quoted” – dash      "Quoted" - dash
6            ½ price …        1/2 price ...
```


:::
:::


Characters with no ASCII spelling (other scripts, emoji) are kept, or
replaced with `sub` when the output must be pure ASCII:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ascii_fold("Tokyo \u6771\u4eac caf\u00e9", sub = "?")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Tokyo ?? cafe"
```


:::
:::


The phonetic codes (`soundex()`, `nysiis()` and the rest) already fold
accented letters internally; fold explicitly before the similarity
functions and before hashing, where `é` and `e` would otherwise differ.

## Standardise words with a dictionary

Abbreviations are the biggest single source of disagreement in addresses
and organisation names. `freplace_tokens()` replaces every whitespace-
separated token found in a dictionary, in one hashed pass per string. An
empty replacement deletes the token, and the result comes back squished.
Strip the punctuation that clings to tokens first:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
addr <- c("12 Smith St.", "3/45 North Rd", "UNIT 7, 9 KING STREET",
          "Flat 2 18 Queen st", "U 5/22 the Esplanade Hwy")
abbrev <- data.frame(
    from = c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "HWY", "CRES", "PDE", "FLAT", "U"),
    to   = c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "HIGHWAY", "CRESCENT", "PARADE",
             "UNIT", "UNIT")
)
std <- freplace_tokens(fgsub("[.,]+", " ", toupper(addr)), abbrev$from, abbrev$to)
data.frame(addr, std)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                      addr                             std
1             12 Smith St.                 12 SMITH STREET
2            3/45 North Rd                 3/45 NORTH ROAD
3    UNIT 7, 9 KING STREET            UNIT 7 9 KING STREET
4       Flat 2 18 Queen st          UNIT 2 18 QUEEN STREET
5 U 5/22 the Esplanade Hwy UNIT 5/22 THE ESPLANADE HIGHWAY
```


:::
:::


Only whole tokens change -- `ST` becomes `STREET`, but `STAR` and `STREET`
itself are left alone -- which is what makes a dictionary approach safe
where `gsub("ST", "STREET", x)` is not. Matching can ignore ASCII case, and
replacements may contain several words. The same mechanism maps name
variants to one canonical form, here a (very) short nickname table:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nick <- data.frame(
    from = c("BILL", "BILLY", "WILL", "BOB", "ROB", "BOBBY", "PEG", "PEGGY",
             "LIZ", "BETH"),
    to   = c("WILLIAM", "WILLIAM", "WILLIAM", "ROBERT", "ROBERT", "ROBERT",
             "MARGARET", "MARGARET", "ELIZABETH", "ELIZABETH")
)
freplace_tokens(c("BILL", "Bob", "peggy", "WILLIAM", "LIZ ANNE"),
                nick$from, nick$to, ignore_case = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "WILLIAM"        "ROBERT"         "MARGARET"       "WILLIAM"        "ELIZABETH ANNE"
```


:::
:::


Dictionaries of thousands of entries cost no more per token than a
dictionary of ten, because each token is one hash lookup. The equivalent
in base R splits every string into a list, matches and pastes back:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
n <- 2e5
words <- c("12", "SMITH", "ST", "RD", "AVE", "UNIT", "MR", "DR", "JOHN",
           "NORTH", "QLD", "4000")
x <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(words, 5, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")

system.time(freplace_tokens(x, abbrev$from, abbrev$to))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   user  system elapsed 
   0.14    0.02    0.06 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
system.time({
    tok <- strsplit(x, " ", fixed = TRUE)
    vapply(tok, function(t) {
        m <- match(t, abbrev$from)
        t[!is.na(m)] <- abbrev$to[m[!is.na(m)]]
        paste(t, collapse = " ")
    }, "")
})
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   user  system elapsed 
   1.79    0.14    1.92 
```


:::
:::


## Restore leading zeros

Spreadsheets and CSV readers turn postcodes, phone numbers and identifiers
into numbers and silently drop their leading zeros -- every Northern
Territory postcode (`0800`-`0899`) comes back as three digits. `fpad()`
puts them back; `side = "right"` pads text for fixed-width exports:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fpad(as.character(c(800, 810, 2000, 4000, 870)), 4, pad = "0")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "0800" "0810" "2000" "4000" "0870"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fpad(c("ID", "NAME", "POSTCODE"), 10, side = "right")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "ID        " "NAME      " "POSTCODE  "
```


:::
:::


Width counts characters, not bytes, so accented text pads correctly too.

## Find the spelling variants

Before matching against anything else, it helps to know how many ways one
value is spelled *within* a column. OpenRefine's **key collision**
clustering does this with a fingerprint: lower-case, fold accents, remove
punctuation, then sort the unique words. Values that share a fingerprint
are almost always the same thing:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
companies <- c("Acme Pty Ltd", "ACME PTY. LTD.", "Ltd Acme Pty", "acme pty ltd ",
               "Acme Holdings", "Bolt & Nut Co", "Bolt and Nut Co",
               "Bolt & Nut Co.", "Cafe Nero", "Caf\u00e9 Nero")
key <- fingerprint(companies)
clusters <- split(companies, key)
clusters[lengths(clusters) > 1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$`acme ltd pty`
[1] "Acme Pty Ltd"   "ACME PTY. LTD." "Ltd Acme Pty"   "acme pty ltd " 

$`bolt co nut`
[1] "Bolt & Nut Co"  "Bolt & Nut Co."

$`cafe nero`
[1] "Cafe Nero" "Café Nero"
```


:::
:::


`"Bolt and Nut Co"` stays out, because the fingerprint deletes `&` but keeps
`and`. A dictionary pass first fixes that, which is the general pattern:
standardise with `freplace_tokens()`, then cluster:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
key2 <- fingerprint(freplace_tokens(companies, "and", "&", ignore_case = TRUE))
split(companies, key2)[["bolt co nut"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Bolt & Nut Co"   "Bolt and Nut Co" "Bolt & Nut Co." 
```


:::
:::


`ngram_fingerprint()` sorts the unique character n-grams instead of words,
so it also joins values that differ by spacing or transposed letters
(`n = 1` is the most forgiving):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ngram_fingerprint(c("Cafe Nero", "CafeNero", "Cafe Neor"), n = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "acefnor" "acefnor" "acefnor"
```


:::
:::


Use the clusters to build the dictionary for `freplace_tokens()`, or as a
deduplication key in their own right.

## A cleaning pipeline

In practice these run as one function applied to each name or address
column before blocking and scoring:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean_name <- function(x) {
    x <- html_unescape(x)
    x <- ascii_fold(x)
    x <- toupper(x)
    x <- fgsub("[^A-Z0-9 ]+", " ", x)
    x <- freplace_tokens(x, c(nick$from, "DR", "MR", "MRS", "MS"),
                         c(nick$to, "", "", "", ""))
    fsquish(x)
}
clean_name(c("  Dr. Fran\u00e7ois  O\u2019Brien-Smith ", "MR BILL  JONES",
             "bob jones"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "FRANCOIS O BRIEN SMITH" "WILLIAM JONES"          "ROBERT JONES"          
```


:::
:::


Every step is parallel and returns unchanged strings without copying them,
so a pipeline like this keeps up with the matching steps that follow
(@sec-uc-link) even at millions of rows.
